Nuclear charge radii of neutron-rich 47–49Sc isotopes were measured using collinear laser spectroscopy at
CERN-ISOLDE. The new data reveal that the charge radii of scandium isotopes exhibit a distinct trend
between N ¼ 20 and N ¼ 28, with 41Sc and 49Sc isotopes having similar values, mirroring the closeness of
the charge radii of 40Ca and 48Ca. Theoretical models that successfully interpret the radii of calcium isotopes
could not account for the observed behavior in scandium radii, in particular the reduced odd-even staggering.
Remarkably, the inclusion of the new 49Sc radius data has unveiled a similar trend in the charge radii of
N ¼ 28 isotones and Z ¼ 20 isotopes when adding the protons atop the 48Ca core and the neutrons atop the
40Ca core, respectively. We demonstrate that this trend is consistent with the prediction of the seniority model.

Nuclear charge radii have provided important informa-
tion on nuclear structure and nuclear models [1–5]. In
particular, high-precision charge radii data across long
isotopic chains are essential for understanding internu-
cleon forces and the nuclear many-body problem [6–8].
Local variations of the charge radii seen in exotic nuclei
with large neutron-to-proton asymmetry often indicate
specific structure effects, such as halo structure [1], shell
closures [6,9,10], and nuclear shape evolution and coex-
istence [3,4,11].
The nuclear charge radii evolution in the Z ¼ 20 region
has long been of interest due to its complex and unique
characteristics. A key feature is the archlike charge radii
trend in calcium isotopes at 20 ≤N ≤28, with almost
identical radii for 40Ca and 48Ca and pronounced odd-even
staggering (OES) [2,6,12,13]. Since its observation in 1984
[12], explaining this radii pattern between 40Ca and 48Ca
has posed a long-standing challenge for nuclear theory; see
Refs. [14,15] for its current interpretation. Another puzzle
is the absence of the expected radii kink at the N ¼ 20 shell
closure, observed in argon (Z ¼ 18), potassium (Z ¼ 19),
and calcium (Z ¼ 20) chains [2,6,12,14,16]. This kink,
however, emerged in scandium (Z ¼ 21) radii at N ¼ 20,
with one proton above the Z ¼ 20 shell closure [17],
prompting further theoretical developments. Why do scan-
dium radii at N ¼ 20 differ so from their neighbors? Do
these differences present across the scandium isotopic
chain from N ¼ 20 to N ¼ 28? How do the radii of
N ¼ 28 isotones with protons filling the 0f7=2 orbital
compare to Z ¼ 20 isotopes with neutrons filling the
0f7=2 orbital, well-isolated from its neighboring orbitals
by magic numbers 20 and 28? To answer these questions,
new charge radii measurements for scandium isotopes near
the N ¼ 28 shell closure are required.
In this Letter, we report the charge radii measurement of
neutron-rich scandium isotopes up to N ¼ 28 using the
COLLAPS collinear laser spectroscopy experiment at
ISOLDE-CERN. Combined with previous data around
N ¼ 20 [17–19], our measurements complete the charge
radius evolution of scandium isotopes between N ¼ 20 and
N ¼ 28. The data reveal a distinct pattern with nearly
identical sizes for 41Sc and 49Sc. Additionally, the new 49Sc
radius provides a key datum for N ¼ 28 isotones, where
protons occupy the 0f7=2 orbital. Our results show that the
radii of N ¼ 28 isotones exhibit a similar archlike proton
number dependence, mirroring the neutron-dependent
trend in calcium. The experimental data are confronted
with nuclear density-functional theory (DFT) and valence-
space in-medium similarity renormalization group (VS-
IMSRG) calculations.
Details of the experiment have been described previously
in Ref. [20]. In brief, radioactive Sc isotopes were produced
by impinging 1.4-GeV protons onto a thick Ta-foil target at
ISOLDE-CERN and selectively ionized using the reso-
nance ionization laser ion source [21]. The ions were
extracted, accelerated to 40 keV, and mass-separated with a
high-resolution mass separator. They were then cooled and
bunched in a gas-filled radio-frequency quadrupole Paul
trap [22], providing ion bunches with a ∼5 μs temporal
width after 100-ms accumulation. The bunched ions deliv-
ered to the COLLAPS setup were resonantly excited via
3d4s 3D1 →3d4p 3F2 transition using a cw frequency-
doubled Ti:Sapphire laser at 364.3 nm. Long-term laser-
frequency stabilization was achieved with a high-accuracy
wavelength meter kept at a constant environmental temper-
ature. The wavelength meter is calibrated in real time by a
diode laser locked to a hyperfine transition of 87Rb. The ion
velocity was tuned to match the Doppler-shifted laser
frequency for the studied Scþ transition. Fluorescence
photons emitted from the laser-excited scandium ions were
detectedby photomultipliers and countedasa function ofthe
tuning velocity to obtain the hyperfine structure (hfs)
spectra. All isotopes were measured alternately with the
reference isotope 45Sc to compensate for remaining velocity
or frequency excursions.

Here, KMS and F are the mass-shift and field-shift factors,
respectively. And M45 and MA are the atomic masses of
45Sc and ASc, respectively.
To calculate δhr2iA;45, the atomic factors KMS and F
must be determined from atomic theory as only one stable
isotope 45Sc is available. In this Letter, F was calculated
with the relativistic Fock-space coupled cluster method
(FSCC) [24,26] in DIRAC program [27], while KMS was
predicted using configuration interaction with many-body
perturbation theory (CI þ MBPT) [25] within the AMBIT
program [28]. The closed-shell Sc3þ [Ar] electron con-
figuration was used for the Dirac-Hartree-Fock reference
state for both methods. The two-particle FSCC sector was
employed in the F calculations where two electrons were
added to the reference state to reach the [Ar]3d4s states of
Scþ. The intermediate Hamiltonian technique [29] was
used to aid convergence, and the two electrons could
occupy orbitals in a model space consisting of the
3d4s4pð4d5s5p4f5d6s6pÞ orbitals, with the intermediate
Hamiltonian space in parentheses. Dyall’s 4z basis set [30]
consisting of 31s21p13d8f6g3h basis functions was used,
including core correlating functions and a layer of diffuse
functions. All electrons were correlated and the virtual
space was cut off at 200 a.u. A Gaussian nuclear charge
distribution [31,32] was used and F was computed from the
numerical derivative of energy calculations at different hr2i
values. For the CI þ MBPT calculations, a B-spline basis
was used, andCI included singleand double excitations from
the 3d4s, 3d2, 4s2, 3d4p, 4s4p, 3d5s, 3d4d configurations
up to 20spdfg, while the MBPT basis consisting of
40spdfgh was used to treat core-valence correlations and
included up to three-body MBPT diagrams. KMS was
calculated using the finite field method, where either the
normal or specific mass-shift operator is added to the
Hamiltonian. The uncertainty was estimated by analyzing
contributions from different computational parameters
[32–34], such as the limited size of the basis set, higher-
order correlation effects, and the relativistic Gaunt term.
Further details are in Ref. [32] and references therein.

With these new results, we can now investigate the
overall charge radii behavior of isotopes with Z ¼ 20  1
and N ¼ 20–28, where valence neutrons occupy the 0f7=2
shell-model orbital. Figure 2(a) compares the experimental
Rch of 40–49Sc, 39–48Ca [6,14], and 38–47K [2]. Several new
features emerge in addition to the puzzling radii kink at
N ¼ 20 in scandium [17], which is not seen in potassium
and calcium. Most remarkably, the radii trend of even-N
scandium isotopes resembles the one seen in calcium above
N ¼ 20. This characteristic trend between N ¼ 20 and
N ¼ 28 is not observed in the potassium chain. Another
notable feature is that the considerable OES seen in calcium
charge radii is much less pronounced in both scandium and
potassium.
To get a better understanding on the observed trend in
scandium radii, we performed calculations using the DFT
and VS-IMSRG methods.
The DFT calculations were performed using two Fayans
energy density functional parametrizations Fy(Δr, HFB)
[37] and Fy(IVP) [38]. The Fy(Δr, HFB) [37] has been
successful in understanding the charge radii of nearly
closed shell nuclei (e.g., K [2], Ca [14], Ni (Z ¼ 28)
[8,9], Cu (Z ¼ 29) [7], Cd (Z ¼ 48) [39], Sn (Z ¼ 50)
[10]) and the open-shell nuclei (e.g., Ge (Z ¼ 32) [40] and
Pd (Z ¼ 46) [41]). The Fy(IVP) is a new functional aiming
to capture the isovector pairing correlations [38]. The
calculations were performed with an axially deformed
DFT solver, which allowed nuclear deformations and
time-odd polarization for odd-Z and odd-N nuclei. For
more details on Fayans DFT methodology and calculations,
see Ref. [17]. As shown in Fig. 2(b), the FyðΔr; HFBÞ
calculations partially capture the δhr2iN;28 trend of scan-
dium when approaching N ¼ 28, although it overestimates
the OES and underestimates the differential radii around
N ¼ 20, as already noted in Ref. [17]. The functional Fy
(IVP) underestimates both OES and differential radii.
The VS-IMSRG calculations use the ΔNNLOGOð394Þ
[42] chiral interaction, which has reasonably reproduced
the differential charge radii of potassium [2] and the
semimagic nickel isotopes [8]. Following the same meth-
odology and parameters as Ref. [17], we decoupled a
1s1=20d3=20f7=21p3=2 valence-space Hamiltonian above a
28Si core to capture the influence of cross-shell excitation
from Z ¼ N ¼ 20 magic shell gap. As seen in Fig. 2(b),
VS-IMSRG predicts almost constant radii for scandium
between N ¼ 20 and N ¼ 28.
Summarizing the results in Fig. 2(b), we conclude that
the current nuclear models used to describe neighboring
isotopic chains with a considerable success [2], fail in
reproducing the observed differential radii trend for scan-
dium isotopes with 19 ≤N ≤28.

Charge radii of 44–49Sc isotopes were determined using
collinear laser spectroscopy. Together with the data of
40–46Sc isotopes [17–19], the scandium radii trend reveals
several intricate features: an unexplained behavior around
N ¼ 20–22, nearly equal charge radii for 41Sc and 49Sc, and
the suppressed OES compared to calcium. Current state-
of-the-art nuclear theories, including Fayans DFT and
VS-IMSRG, are unable to fully reproduce this trend,
highlighting the need for further theoretical improvements.
To study the effect of the 0f7=2 shell occupation in
semimagic Z ¼ 20 isotopes and N ¼ 28 isotones, we
analyzed the relative charge radii Δr2
ch. Remarkably, the
radii of N ¼ 28 isotones exhibit a seniority-limit pattern
almost identical to that of the calcium chain. This feature,
nicely captured by the DFT calculation using FyðΔr; HFBÞ
and Fy(IVP), strongly supports the validity of the seniority
coupling scheme in this region.
